chapter_theme: The poem moves from the lord's age and the land to Kausambi, King Sathanikan and Queen Mirukavathi, then tells how a bird carries the queen to her father the sage, how her son Udayanan is born and grows up in the hermitage with Yugi, wins a lute and a divine elephant, and how his uncle Vikraman and then his father Sathanikan hand him a throne and turn ascetic, ending with his crowning and four ministers.

cast.role: the lord, a tirthankara, at whose time the story is set
king of the Vatsa land at Kausambi, Udayanan's father
the huge bird that carries off the queen
the queen's father, a sage in the hill forest
the queen's son, born in the hermitage
Udayanan's friend and later minister, son of the yogi Brahmasundaran
the divine elephant tamed by Udayanan's lute
King Vikraman, the queen's brother, who gives his kingdom to Udayanan

5.reading: The poet turns to the age when the lord of the three ramparts, fair Veeranathan, pours a rain of virtue on this crowded earth, and says he will tell of the land of a king who rules in that time.
5.nuance: Virtue falls as rain from the tirthankara here, where the Kural makes the rain follow the king's justice; the poem sets its king inside the lord's age.

6.reading: The poet says the jambu-named continent, ringed by seas each twice as wide as the one inside it, is like a fine gem among the islands.

7.reading: Within the Bharata part of that continent, in its land of dharma, the poet places the Vatsa country, where the wind carries the scent of its groves.
7.nuance: The first two lines compare the land to a bow drawn with a string; the figure is hard to follow, and only the placing of Vatsa in Bharata's dharma-land is firm.

8.reading: The poet says the heavenly world, seeing the limitless beauty of the city, calls it with a hand of tall flags to come without fear.
8.nuance: Who calls whom is not clear in the Tamil: the heaven may call the city up, or the city's flags may call the gods down. Either way the city is praised as the match of heaven.

9.reading: The poet names the city Kausambi, where men and women in cloud-high mansions live in pleasure by day and night.
9.nuance: The city is praised by its pleasure, not its virtue, and the poem will later make renunciation the end of such a life.

10.reading: The poet introduces King Sathanikan, spear-bearing, as generous as a rain-cloud and as rich as Kubera.

11.reading: The poet names the king's beloved queen, delicate as a peahen and as faithful as Arundhati, Mirukavathi.
11.nuance: Her fidelity is praised by the comparison to Arundhati, the star-wife, before any event shows it.

12.reading: The chaste queen, in the ninth month after a good soul had entered her womb, sits one day on a fine couch.
12.nuance: A virtuous being 'taking birth' in her womb is told as a plain fact of rebirth; no earlier life is named for him here.
12.event: Mirukavathi, in the ninth month of pregnancy, sits on her couch.

13.reading: As the queen sleeps in a red cloth on the moonlit terrace, a huge bird seizes her, taking her for flesh, and flies up.
13.nuance: The bird's mistake is the whole cause; no fault of hers or the king's is named.
13.event: A huge bird seizes the sleeping Mirukavathi and carries her into the sky.

14.reading: The bird sets her down in the forest where her father, now a great sage, lives; she wakes, and the bird, which does not eat the life it seized, flies off.
14.nuance: The same bird that was a menace in the last verse is shown to be harmless; the verse says it did not eat the life it had seized.
14.event: The bird sets Mirukavathi down by her father the sage and flies away without harming her.

15.reading: With the child ripening, the queen suffers pains, and on a day the planets look kindly the son is born, like a pearl from a conch.
15.event: Mirukavathi bears a son on an auspicious day.

16.reading: Learning where she has come, the queen grieves, then sees her son lying like a gem and her sorrow ebbs with love; her father the sage comes and sees them.
16.nuance: Line 1 has a damaged word in the queen's description, and its first half is hard to join to the rest; the grief and the sage's arrival are clear.
16.event: The sage comes and finds his daughter and her newborn son.

17.reading: The sage takes mother and child to his hermitage and tends them; the boy, born like the sun rising, is named Udayanan, and they stay with the sages.
17.nuance: The name 'rising' fits the verse's comparison of his birth to a sunrise.
17.event: The sage brings Mirukavathi and her son to the hermitage, where the boy is named Udayanan.

18.reading: Udayanan, born to the royal line, and Yugi, son of the yogi Brahmasundaran, grow up together, master the arts, and by the sage's grace Udayanan gains Indra's lute.
18.nuance: The lute comes as a gift of grace from the sage, not of his own skill, and it sets up the elephant scene.
18.event: Udayanan and Yugi grow up together and he receives Indra's lute from the sage.

19.reading: Seeing a mountain-like divine elephant, the youth plays his lute; the elephant listens, bows at his feet and offers its trunk, and he mounts it and rides to the hermitage.
19.nuance: Music, not force, tames the elephant, the first sign of the lute's power.
19.event: Udayanan plays the lute, tames the divine elephant and rides it to the hermitage.

20.reading: The elephant pledges to him in a dream that, though a keeper mount it, it will not stay with him on the day he eats before it; he hears this.
20.nuance: The condition of the pledge turns on a hard sentence in lines 2 and 3; the sense given is the likeliest, not certain.
20.event: The elephant pledges itself to Udayanan in a dream.

21.reading: At that time King Vikraman, son of a sage, grieving that he has no children, comes and sits worshipping the sage's feet.
21.event: Vikraman, childless, comes to worship the sage's feet.

22.reading: Asking whose sons these are, he hears the sage's answer, gladly crowns the boy and gives him his retinue, and says he will take up the ascetic life.
22.nuance: Line 1 has a damaged word ('ராமி'), so who is said to be whose son has to be taken from the next lines, where he gives up kingship to the boy.
22.event: Vikraman learns who the boys are, crowns Udayanan and resolves to become an ascetic.

23.reading: Vikraman gets his sister and the sage's leave, seats the boy on a fierce elephant, hands his own kingdom to his sister's son, and goes into the forest as an ascetic.
23.nuance: He ends his childlessness by making his sister's son the heir, and the same act is his turn to renunciation; the kingdom passes to a sister's son, not a son of his own.
23.event: Vikraman gives his kingdom to his nephew Udayanan and becomes a forest ascetic.

24.reading: Udayanan, grown into a handsome youth, rules justly with a straight sceptre; Sathanikan, pining for the queen, speaks of one fault he has seen.
24.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure: what the fault is, and whose, is not stated in the verse.
24.event: Udayanan rules justly; Sathanikan, longing for his queen, names a fault.

25.reading: Hearing of the queen's return and the prince's going, the king is glad and enters the city; the queen joins him and bears two sons like young gods.
25.event: Sathanikan welcomes Mirukavathi back and she bears two sons.

26.reading: The king names the two sons Pingalan and Katakan and rules the land lovingly, while Udayanan and Yugi go out and bring all the lands there under their sway.
26.event: Sathanikan names his sons; Udayanan and Yugi conquer the surrounding lands.

27.reading: Sathanikan calls Udayanan, gives him the throne of the earth, and himself takes up ascetic life, freed from anger and cares, and stands in yoga.
27.nuance: The king chooses the throne's heir, Udayanan, over the two sons he has just named, and leaves while still living, not at death.
27.event: Sathanikan hands the throne to Udayanan and becomes a yoga-practising ascetic.

claims.claim: the ascetic's life frees a man from anger and cares

28.reading: At his coronation Udayanan becomes lord of the Vatsa people, with four ministers around him: Yugi, Urumannuvan, Vayantakan and Vidapakan.
28.nuance: Line 2 has the second minister's name broken in word division, and the reading 'Urumannuvan' is taken from that.
28.event: Udayanan is crowned king of the Vatsa people and four ministers are named.

links.note: The seizing bird that threatens the queen in verse 13 is shown in verse 14 to set her down unharmed.
links.teaches: The bird's danger in 13 is answered in 14, so the abduction is told as a passage to the hermitage and not as an injury.

links.note: The lute the youth receives from the sage in verse 18 is the instrument that tames the elephant in 19.
links.teaches: The gift of grace in 18 is shown working at once, so the lute is the means by which Udayanan wins allies.

links.note: The elephant that bows at his lute in verse 19 pledges itself to him in a dream in verse 20.
links.teaches: The taming ends in a bond of loyalty, so the music wins a companion and not only a mount.

links.note: Vikraman's resolve to take up ascetic life in verse 22 is carried out in verse 23 when he goes into the forest.
links.teaches: A resolve voiced in one verse is kept in the next, with the kingdom handed over first.

links.note: Vikraman's grief at having no child (verse 21) meets the Kural's praise of children who know what should be known, and the epic gives him a sister's son in place of his own.
links.teaches: The epic shows that the heir the Kural praises can come by a sister's son, not only by birth, and that the want of a child can lead to renunciation.

gains.a: The verse's grief at being childless gets a standard by which an heir is valued, which the epic's king only feels as loss.
gains.b: The couplet's praise of knowing children gets a case where the lack of one's own child is answered by taking a nephew as heir.

links.note: Vikraman gives up his kingdom and goes to the forest, as the quatrain's best of men renounce home and wealth on seeing they do not last.
links.teaches: The epic shows a king doing what the quatrain says, with the order of arranging his heir first and then leaving, which the quatrain does not mention.

gains.a: The epic's king gets the reason for his act, the failing of home and wealth, which the verse does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain's renouncer gets a concrete case, a king who provides for his kingdom before he goes.

links.note: Vikraman leaves his kingdom to a nephew he has just found, while the Cintamani's Lokamapalan sets his young son on the throne and takes the ascetics' guise.
links.teaches: Both epics tell of a king handing over rule and turning ascetic, but here the heir is a sister's son and the turn follows childlessness, where the Cintamani's follows the setting up of his own son.

links.note: Sathanikan crowns the heir first and then turns ascetic, in the order the Cintamani's chariot-king lays down: guard the kingdom, give it to a worthy son, and only then renounce.
links.teaches: The Cintamani states as advice the order that this king follows in the story, and the epic adds that he passes over his two named sons for Udayanan.

links.note: Sathanikan gives up the throne while living, where the quatrain says kings under the umbrella on elephants are carried off as dead.
links.teaches: The epic's king keeps his rank by choosing to leave it before death, which the quatrain does not allow for.

gains.a: The king's leaving gets a sharper meaning, since the quatrain says death is how all kings finally lose the umbrella.
gains.b: The quatrain's claim that none escape gets a qualification: one can leave the throne by renouncing before it is taken.

links.note: Veeranathan's rain of virtue in verse 5 is set beside the Kural's rain that comes where the king rules justly.
links.teaches: The epic gives the rain to the tirthankara's teaching, where the Kural makes it the reward of the ruler's sceptre.

gains.a: The epic's rain of virtue gets the Kural's older idea that rain follows the justice of the ruler.
gains.b: The couplet's rain of justice gets a second source: the lord's dharma, not the king, brings the fall.

source_issues: Verse 12, line 2: a pulli after a vowel sign was removed by the repair step.
Verse 16, line 1: the word 'கண்ணினாடான்' is damaged; the sense is taken from the rest of the verse.
Verse 22, line 1: 'ராமி' is damaged and gives no clear sense.
Verse 28, line 2: the minister's name 'சாருரு மண்ணு வாவும்' is broken across words; read as Urumannuvan.
The poem's named lord at verse 5 is Veeranathan, a form of Mahavira.
